past.vs: Revenue $28.24bn, +26% vs a year earlier, vs $27.58bn consensus (Tesla-compiled). Adjusted EPS $0.33 vs $0.55 consensus (Tesla-compiled; a 40% miss); GAAP EPS $0.32, helped by a ~$1bn gain on Tesla's SpaceX shares.
past.guide: No numeric guidance. Capex above $25bn for 2026 and rising for 2-3 years; free cash flow under pressure in the second half; energy margin to settle in the low-to-mid 20s % over the long term.
past.reaction: −14.5% on 23 Jul vs −1.2% for the S&P 500 (worst day in nearly a year).
take: Volume back, profit not. Deliveries 480,126 (+25% vs a year earlier, a Q2 record), but operating profit $398m (−57%), a 1.4% operating margin vs 4.1% a year earlier.

Car margin: better than a year ago, worse than last quarter. Automotive gross margin excluding regulatory credits 16.3% vs 15.0% a year earlier, but down from 19.2% in Q1 2026, which one-off warranty and tariff gains had lifted. Average selling prices fell, and low-rate financing helped volume.
Regulatory credits nearly gone: $146m vs $439m a year earlier, after US fuel-economy fines were scrapped (chain C4).
Spending boom: capex $5.79bn (+142%); free cash flow −$1.09bn, the first negative quarter since early 2024; up to $30bn of debt facilities being arranged (chain C1).
Energy: 13.5 GWh deployed (+41% vs a year earlier); energy gross margin 20.4% after a $240m one-off warranty charge.
Software: about 1.5m paying FSD customers (+56%); 55% of North American deliveries had FSD enabled.

Robotaxi and Cybercab: Cybercab production started in Texas; unsupervised robotaxi rides expanded to Miami, Orlando and Tampa. But the fleet is still small (about a dozen cars or fewer per city) and paid robotaxi miles (about 2.4m in total by June vs 1.8m in March) grew more slowly late in the quarter.
past.impact: Demand indicators strong (DM1, DM4a, DM4b); margin and cash pressure feed the quality check and chains C1 and C4; forecasts cut sharply since (DM2).

lead: Tesla is Building history (today's zone: Sell), at −35 on a −100 to +100 scale, 5 points below the −30 Sell line and up from −37 on 7 Oct (and from −54 on 2 Oct): only Liquidity moved today (to +13 from 0, as Fed rate expectations turned bullish). Q3 deliveries were flat, China sales are falling and the shares cost about 12 times the peer median on expected profit, while the price trend stayed improved from 2 Oct even though the shares slipped 0.74% today. Caution: on Tesla, past Sell readings driven by price trend often came near lows.
bullets: Demand has turned slightly negative. Demand scores −11: Q3 deliveries −2.1% and storage deployed +9.6% (Jul-Sep vs a year earlier), both neutral; Tesla's China retail sales −18.2% (Jun-Aug vs a year earlier, bearish); analysts' 2027 profit forecast $2.15 a share vs $2.59 90 days ago (−17.2%, bearish). Still positive: revenue grew 25.5% in the June quarter vs a year earlier against a 3.1% average for the prior four, and gross margin was 18.6% over the last 4 quarters vs 17.5% for the 4 a year earlier (one-offs removed).

Valuation is extreme on every measure. Valuation scores −100: forward P/E 182.7x vs a 15.6x peer median (+1,073%, down from +1,107% on 7 Oct); growth-adjusted P/E 4.5 vs 1.2 (+262%); EV/EBITDA 135.2x vs 20.6x (+556%); trailing P/E 347.2x vs its own median of 215.8x (+61%; only about 2 years of history, see Known defects). The market is paying for robotaxis, robots and energy, not today's car profits.

Money flows are mixed. Liquidity scores +13, up from 0 on 7 Oct: buying vs selling volume 1.06x over 20 days (neutral); funds added a net 1.22% of shares last quarter (bullish); the dollar index rose 3.05 points in 20 trading days (bearish); the market's net odds of a Fed cut vs a rise at the next meeting moved 17.0 points towards a cut vs four weeks earlier (bullish, now past the 15-point line; now 1% cut vs 16% rise, a month ago 2% vs 34%); only 1.9% of tradable shares are sold short, below the 2% floor.

The price trend is still −32 and negative. Price trend scores −32 (−100 on 2 Oct, unchanged from 7 Oct): the price is 4.1% below its 200-day average (neutral), the 50-day average is 9.7% below the 200-day (bearish), and the 3-month return trails the peers by 3.5 points (neutral). The shares closed at $375.00, −0.74% on the day vs −0.47% for the S&P 500, and are up 5.9% over 5 trading days.

Not confirmed: day 5 of 10. The call needs 7 of 10 trading days in one zone. The score rose from −54 (2 Oct) to −37 (5 Oct) because the price rose: the 200-day-average and peer-relative-strength readings both moved from bearish to neutral. It stayed at −37 on 6 Oct and 7 Oct, then rose to −35 on 8 Oct as Liquidity improved.
defects: Live from 4 Oct 2026 (promoted from staging; history starts fresh on production): the call needs 7 of the last 10 trading days in one zone before it is confirmed.

Caution from the 5-year replay: on Tesla, Sell and Strong Sell days were followed by its best returns, +23 to +28 points vs the S&P 500 over the next 6 months, beating it on about 7 in 10 days. Tesla swings so hard that a trend-following score turns Sell near lows. Treat a Sell reading driven by price trend as weak evidence on its own.

Nvidia's +17.2% over 3 months pulls the peer average up: with all 8 peers Tesla trails by 3.2 points (neutral); without Nvidia it would be roughly level with the other seven (also neutral). The earlier composite estimate without Nvidia (about −47) has not been recomputed for today. Kenneth chose to keep all 8 peers (3 Oct).

quality_info.name: Dilution
quality_info.value: 424m restricted performance shares awarded to Musk (10.7% of the 3.95bn shares) were issued in late 2025 and are already in the share count; they vest only if very large targets are hit. A further ~286m net shares were issued in Jun 2026 when Musk exercised his 2018 options.

quality_info.name: Customer concentration
quality_info.value: None: Tesla sells to millions of consumers; no customer is 10%+ of revenue.

CAR.sells: New Tesla cars (Model 3, Model Y, Cybertruck, Cybercab; Model S and X production ended in 2026) sold outright.
CAR.buyers: Consumers worldwide, plus fleets and rental firms, sold directly by Tesla (no dealers).
pos: Still the engine: 70% of sales over the last 4 quarters, growing again (+9.6% vs the 4 quarters before; +26.7% in the June quarter vs a year earlier).
Each car is a future customer for FSD subscriptions, Supercharging and insurance (Services).
neg: Not recurring: sold once, and volume swings with prices, incentives and subsidies.

Cheap financing helped 2026 volume and average prices fell. Car sales earn below the company gross margin (see the car-sales margin); in the June quarter the automotive margin excluding credits was 16.3%, up from 15.0% a year earlier but down from Q1's one-off-boosted 19.2%.
Exposed to the China price war, tariffs and memory costs (chains C1, C5).

CRD.sells: Regulatory credits sold to other carmakers that miss emissions or fuel-economy rules.
pos: Almost pure profit when sold: no cost of goods (shown with car sales because Tesla reports their cost together).
neg: Disappearing: −39.8% over the last 4 quarters vs the 4 before, and $146m in the June quarter vs $439m a year earlier, after US fuel-economy fines were scrapped (chain C4).
Its loss hits gross profit almost one-for-one.

LSE.sells: Cars leased to customers (Tesla keeps ownership).
LSE.buyers: Consumers and businesses that lease rather than buy.
pos: Recurring monthly payments, and leasing has its own, much higher margin than car sales.
neg: Small and shrinking: 1.5% of sales, −11.3% vs the 4 quarters before.

SVC.sells: Services and other: FSD subscriptions, Supercharging, insurance, used cars, repairs, parts and merchandise.
SVC.buyers: Tesla owners (and other EV drivers at Superchargers).
pos: Fastest-growing part: +34.0% over the last 4 quarters vs the 4 before; 14.6% of sales now vs 7.8% three years ago.
Partly recurring (FSD subscriptions, charging, insurance): about 1.5m paying FSD customers at the June quarter, and future FSD sales will mostly be subscriptions.
Margin rising fast: 10.9% (last 4 quarters) vs 5.6% a year earlier.
neg: Still earns below the company gross margin (10.9% vs 18.9%), because used cars and repairs are low-margin.
Robotaxi revenue would land here, but the fleet is still small (about a dozen cars or fewer per city in mid-2026).

ENE.sells: Battery storage (Megapack for utilities, Powerwall for homes) and solar.
ENE.buyers: Utilities, power developers and data centres; homeowners.
pos: Most profitable part: 29.4% gross margin (last 4 quarters) vs 18.9% for the company, up from 13.0% three years ago.
Growing: +16.8% over the last 4 quarters vs the 4 before; 12.4% of sales vs 5.8% three years ago. Storage deployed +40.6% in the June quarter vs a year earlier.
AI data centres need large batteries, a fresh source of demand.
neg: Lumpy: deployments swing quarter to quarter with big projects.
June-quarter margin dropped to 20.4% after a $240m one-off warranty charge; management expects the low-to-mid 20s % over the long term, below the last-4-quarter 29.4%.
Battery cells are scarce: management named battery capacity a limit (chain C1).

shift.title: What the shift means for Tesla
pos: Tesla is slowly becoming less of a pure carmaker: car sales fell from 82% to 70% of revenue in 3 years (last 4 quarters vs the 4 quarters to Jun 2023), while energy rose from 6% to 12% and services from 8% to 15%.
Energy is the profit bright spot: its gross margin rose from 13.0% to 29.4% over the same 3 years, well above the company's 18.9%.
Company gross margin is up from 17.5% to 18.9% (last 4 quarters vs the 4 a year earlier), helped by energy and services margins.
neg: Over 3 years margins fell: derived by difference from SEC figures, the automotive margin was about 23.4% and the company gross margin about 21.5% in the 4 quarters to Jun 2023, vs 18.9% for the company now (the engine shows the 3-year figures as blank, see the note).

The shift is not lifting margins on its own: the mix change alone took about 0.3 points off gross margin vs a year earlier (each part's margin held at that earlier level), because low-margin services grew fastest.
Regulatory credits, almost pure profit, are fading out (1.4% of sales, −39.8% vs the 4 quarters before).
Cars are still 70% of sales, so car pricing and incentives still decide most of the profit.
